summary: This note traces the history of the Bank of England £1 note. A new series C design appeared in 1960, replacing the old notes, which ceased to be legal tender in 1962, and featured Queen Elizabeth II on the front. Series D notes followed from 1978 with Isaac Newton on the back, and in 1981 the government announced the note would be replaced by a one pound coin, which was introduced in 1983 before the note lost legal tender status in 1988.
one_line: History of the Bank of England £1 note, from the series C and D designs to its replacement by the one pound coin in 1983.
key_facts: A new design for one pound notes was introduced in 1960.
The old one pound notes ceased to be legal tender in 1962.
Series C notes were slightly narrower than the earlier notes and were the first one pound notes to feature a portrait of Queen Elizabeth II on the front.
The reverse design of the series C notes incorporated the logo of the Bank of England.
Series C notes were replaced by series D notes from 1978 onward.
Series D notes featured Queen Elizabeth II on the front and scientist Isaac Newton on the back.
The series D note was redesigned slightly in 1981 to feature brighter background colours.
On 31 July 1981 it was announced that the one pound note would be replaced by a one pound coin, following a consultation with retailers and other groups.
Notes on average lasted only nine months in general circulation, while coins could last forty years or more.
The government believed the growing vending industry would benefit from a one pound coin.
The new cupro-nickel one pound coin was introduced on 21 April 1983.
The one pound note ceased to be legal tender on 11 March 1988.
